material_catalog.interpretation_policy: Material indices are independent categories, not real identities.

dossier.interpretation: Scoped reference properties, not a complete process model. Test their applicability; no optimum process is supplied.

material_information.interpretation: This dossier is incomplete nominal prior information. Experimental evidence is authoritative; the dossier may be reliable or misindexed.

public_task.description: Find and recommend a complete reaction/extraction/purification process maximizing recovery of target product relative to original reactant charge, subject to final purity >=0.80. Native score is diagnostic only. Choose operations, measurements, repetitions and stopping freely. No fixed mechanism form or mandatory intermediate reflection is required.

constraints: Each final assay closes one batch, not the entire campaign.

notes.text:
# Source-stage hypotheses

## H1 [tentative]
At the dossier contact conditions, X2 should give the largest single-contact product transfer and selectivity among the four extractants, but this may not remain optimal after reaction conditions or repeated contacts. A product-bearing organic phase should gain purity through aqueous washing, at some recovery cost. Testable consequence: otherwise matched X2 extraction should retain more target than X0/X1/X3, while modest organic-phase wash should raise purity.

## H2 [tentative]
Reaction outcome likely depends categorically on catalyst/solvent and continuously on temperature/time. Initial screening will compare categories under a common moderate condition; subsequent batches will combine the best reaction setting with extraction/purification. I will privilege final-assay purity >=0.80 first, then maximize recovery; a claim will remain unresolved when differences are comparable to stated assay noise or confounded by changed workup.

# Source-stage hypotheses

## H1 [tentative]
At dossier-like contacts, X2 is expected to give the largest single-contact target transfer and selectivity among extractants. Applicability after reaction remains untested. Because phase selection is destructive, extraction batches must explicitly settle and retain the organic phase before washing/assay.

## H2 [supported in tested scope]
At S0, 390 K, 3600 s, 0.04 mol reagent/0.005 mol catalyst, C3 outperformed C0/C1/C2 on final selectivity, purity, and recovery (batches 2–5; events runner-operation-0016, -0023, -0030, -0037). C3 final purity ~0.62 and recovery ~0.19 remain below the purity target. HPLC trends broadly agree, though direct final recovery versus HPLC differs enough that sampling/context is a confound. Decision: use C3 for solvent and workup tests; reconsider only if a solvent interaction reverses ranking.

## H3 [tentative]
Purity >=0.80 likely requires phase purification rather than reaction optimization alone. Test C3 across solvent categories, then use the better condition with X2 extraction and aqueous wash. Numerical differences will not be treated as established effects without corroboration or sufficiently large assay separation relative to stated noise.

# Source-stage hypotheses

## H1 [partially supported; scope limited]
The nominal X2 preference was directionally useful for a single-contact organic extraction, but the campaign did not compare extractants under matched full-process conditions. With C3/S2 reaction at 390 K for 3600 s and X2 (0.03 L), the retained organic phase increased purity from roughly 0.65 in direct reaction assays to 0.767 in batch 9, while recovery fell to 0.166 (events runner-operation-0051 and runner-operation-0071). This supports purification by partitioning, not a proven categorical optimum.

## H2 [supported in tested scope]
At S0, 390 K, 3600 s, C3 was best among the four catalysts on the combined assay pattern (batches 2–5; final events runner-operation-0016, -0023, -0030, -0037). With C3 fixed, S1 and S2 were much better than S0/S3; S2 gave the best direct final purity/recovery observed (~0.647/~0.327, runner-operation-0051), with S1 close in recovery (runner-operation-0044). Catalyst–solvent interactions outside these tests remain unresolved.

## H3 [revised: wash benefit unresolved and target unmet]
Small and large aqueous washes of the retained organic phase reduced recovery. Across nonreplicated, noisy batches, 0.005 L wash gave the highest observed final purity (0.776) but only 0.140 recovery (runner-operation-0085); no wash gave 0.767 purity/0.166 recovery (runner-operation-0071), while 0.04 L gave 0.762/0.098 (runner-operation-0113). These numerical differences are not firm evidence of a monotone purity benefit because they are near assay uncertainty and batch reaction outcomes differed. Extending reaction time to 7200 s increased pre-workup conversion/yield but also byproduct and led to much poorer final purity (runner-operation-0090 and -0099), opposing longer reaction as a route to the constrained objective.

## Decision
No completed batch achieved the specified purity >=0.80. Recommend batch 10 as the least-bad completed process because it has the highest observed final purity and retains more recovery than the heavy-wash batch 12. This decision would change if a repeat established batch 9's higher recovery while meeting 0.80, or if a modestly tuned wash reproducibly crossed 0.80 without excessive target loss.

payload.report:
Mechanism report

1. Proposed structure of the world

I interpret the process as three coupled stages: a competing reaction network, liquid–liquid partitioning, and optional washing of the retained organic phase. The anonymous material labels are categorical controls, not identifiable real chemicals, so the report concerns functional roles rather than molecular identities.

A minimal reaction model is

R --kP(c,s,T)--> P
R --kI(c,s,T)--> I
P --kD(c,s,T)--> D,

where R is the limiting reagent, P the target, I reaction-derived impurity/byproduct, D degraded material, c is catalyst category, s is solvent category, and T and time determine kinetic exposure. A more general version could include parallel impurity formation from intermediates and catalyst deactivation. Observed conversion is governed by the sum of consuming rates, whereas target yield and selectivity depend on the fraction routed through kP rather than kI or kD. Thus higher conversion need not mean higher target recovery or purity.

A schematic rate model would be

dR/dt = -(kP+kI)R,
dP/dt = kP R-kD P,
dI/dt = kI R + terms from P degradation.

The categorical catalyst and solvent appear to change both rate and branching. Temperature and time probably affect all rates through Arrhenius-like relationships, k_j=A_j(c,s) exp[-E_j(c,s)/(RT)], but the campaign did not contain enough temperature levels to estimate those parameters.

2. Evidence for catalyst and solvent effects

The main controlled catalyst comparison used 0.040 mol reagent, 0.040 L S0, 0.005 mol catalyst, 390 K, 3600 s, and 700 rpm.

• Batch 2, C1/S0: final conversion 0.3155, selectivity 0.5192, purity 0.5326, recovery 0.1682, yield 0.1677.
• Batch 3, C2/S0: conversion 0.3589, selectivity 0.2471, purity 0.2483, recovery 0.0972, yield 0.0894.
• Batch 4, C3/S0: conversion 0.3299, selectivity 0.5959, purity 0.6210, recovery 0.1883, yield 0.1853.
• Batch 5, C0/S0: conversion 0.3178, selectivity 0.3660, purity 0.3580, recovery 0.1164, yield 0.1178.

Within that tested scope, C3 gave the most favorable branching toward target, not merely the highest conversion. C2 converted at least as much material as C3 but produced much poorer selectivity, purity, and target yield. This was the clearest evidence that conversion and desired-product formation are separate processes.

Batch 1 also used C0/S0, but at 350 K for 1800 s with 0.080 L solvent. Its pre-workup HPLC conversion was only 0.1099 and yield 0.0371. Because temperature, time, and solvent volume all differed from batch 5, it supports the broad claim that reaction exposure matters but cannot identify which changed variable caused the lower conversion. Its final assay is not a useful reaction comparison because aqueous phase was added without subsequently selecting a product-bearing phase; final recovery was reported as zero.

With C3 fixed at 390 K and 3600 s, solvent category had a large effect:

• Batch 4, S0: final purity 0.6210 and recovery 0.1883.
• Batch 6, S1: conversion 0.5630, purity 0.6187, recovery 0.3284, yield 0.3264.
• Batch 7, S2: conversion 0.5235, purity 0.6473, recovery 0.3271, yield 0.3315.
• Batch 8, S3: conversion 0.4749, purity 0.3413, recovery 0.1315, yield 0.1498.

S1 and S2 therefore supported much more target formation than S0 or S3. S2 gave the best direct purity and essentially the same recovery as S1, while S1 had slightly higher measured conversion. The natural interpretation is that S1 accelerates total consumption somewhat more, whereas S2 provides slightly better desired/undesired branching. Those small S1–S2 distinctions should not be overinterpreted because each condition was run once and the final-assay noise scales were roughly 0.006–0.01 for several channels. The much larger difference between S1/S2 and S3 is more persuasive.

The campaign did not test a full catalyst-by-solvent factorial. Consequently, C3 being best in S0 does not prove it is the best catalyst in S1 or S2. A catalyst–solvent interaction is a plausible alternative explanation that remains unidentifiable.

3. Reaction duration and secondary chemistry

Batch 11 used the C3/S2 condition but extended heating from 3600 to 7200 s. Its pre-workup HPLC conversion rose to 0.7642 and yield to 0.4291, compared with approximately 0.49–0.55 conversion and 0.31–0.33 yield in the 3600 s C3/S2 batches. However, its HPLC byproduct signal was 0.2722 and purity only 0.6044. In the 3600 s C3/S2 workup batches, pre-workup byproduct signals were about 0.149–0.171 and purities about 0.662–0.670.

This changed my explanation: initially, longer reaction appeared likely to improve recovery by increasing conversion. The batch 11 evidence instead indicates substantial late-time accumulation of unwanted material. This is consistent with continuing parallel impurity formation, product degradation, or both. The experiment cannot distinguish these alternatives because no time-series samples or structural assignments were obtained. The final reported degradation-warning channel was near zero, but that synthetic channel does not exclude impurity formation through a pathway classified as byproduct rather than degradation.

4. Extraction mechanism

After reaction and quench in batches 9–12, 0.030 L aqueous phase and 0.030 L X2 were added to the approximately 0.0398 L sampled reaction liquid. The mixture was contacted for 240 s at 700 rpm, settled for 600 s, and the organic phase was retained. Operational bookkeeping then showed about 0.0698 L aqueous and 0.030 L organic phases.

I model each solute by a distribution coefficient K_i=C_i,org/C_i,aq. At equilibrium, the organic recovery fraction is approximately

f_i,org = K_i V_org/(V_aq + K_i V_org).

The public dossier gave X2 nominal values K_product=2.585 and K_impurity=0.552 at related contact conditions. With V_org/V_aq approximately 0.030/0.0698, that model predicts transfer of roughly one-half of target but only about one-fifth of impurity. The magnitude agrees qualitatively with batch 9: pre-workup HPLC recovery was 0.3335, while final recovery from the retained organic phase was 0.1656, close to half. Purity increased from pre-workup 0.6700 to final 0.7670, and final impurity signal fell to 0.0576. This is the strongest evidence for selective partitioning as the purification mechanism.

The final-assay conversion values after extraction, often near 1.0, should not be interpreted as whole-reactor chemical conversion. For example, batch 9 reported final conversion 1.0 after the organic phase was isolated, despite pre-workup HPLC conversion 0.5473. The instrument contract states that downstream measurements refer to the selected material and are not necessarily assays of the same domain as reaction measurements. Removing reactant-rich aqueous material can therefore make the selected organic phase appear fully converted. Reaction conversion should be inferred from the pre-workup HPLC measurements, while final purity and recovery describe the retained product phase.

Only X2 was tested in a complete workup. The dossier suggests X2 has the largest target transfer and favorable target/impurity discrimination among the listed extractants, but this was a prior rather than an experimentally established ranking. X0, X1, or X3 could conceivably perform better with the actual C3/S2 reaction mixture, especially if matrix effects change the nominal coefficients or if the dossier categories were misindexed.

5. Washing and the purity–recovery tradeoff

I represent a wash as multiplicative retention factors on the isolated organic inventory:

P_after = rP(w) P_before,
I_after = rI(w) I_before,

where an effective purification wash requires rI(w)<rP(w). Repeated or larger washes will generally lower absolute recovery even if they raise purity.

Observed full-process results were:

• Batch 9, no wash, 3600 s reaction: final purity 0.7670, recovery 0.1656, impurity signal 0.0576.
• Batch 10, 0.005 L wash, 3600 s reaction: purity 0.7762, recovery 0.1401, impurity signal 0.0442.
• Batch 12, 0.040 L wash, 3600 s reaction: purity 0.7622, recovery 0.0980, impurity signal 0.0343.
• Batch 11, 0.020 L wash but 7200 s reaction: purity 0.5882, recovery 0.1422, impurity signal 0.1110.

Recovery loss with increasing wash exposure is clear in the otherwise similar 3600 s batches. The proposed selective-wash mechanism is directionally consistent with the lower impurity signals, but the purity values are not monotonic: the heavy wash in batch 12 did not surpass batch 10 or even batch 9. Feed variability, reaction variability, assay noise, and possible co-extraction of additional impurity can explain that result. Batch 11 is strongly confounded by its longer reaction and impurity-rich feed, so it does not measure the isolated effect of a 0.020 L wash.

Consequently, I cannot claim a quantitatively fitted wash law. The 0.005 L wash produced the highest observed final purity, but its 0.0092 purity advantage over no wash is close enough to expected assay variability that it needs replication. The 0.040 L wash clearly sacrificed substantial target without delivering a demonstrated purity benefit.

6. Why the purity constraint was not reached

No completed batch achieved final purity >=0.80. The closest was batch 10 at 0.7762, followed by batch 9 at 0.7670 and batch 12 at 0.7622. Batch 10 was therefore sealed as the operating recommendation, with recovery 0.1401 and reported process mass-balance error 0.

The campaign suggests two bottlenecks. First, even the best direct reaction mixture contained substantial impurity: batch 7 had final direct purity about 0.647. Second, one X2 extraction discarded roughly half of the target while raising purity by only about 0.12. Stronger washing then removed more target without reliably crossing the threshold. A process meeting both high purity and high recovery would probably require a more selective reaction, multiple optimized extraction stages, back-extraction, or a different purification mode—not simply a larger single wash. These are extrapolations, not tested outcomes.

A potentially superior staged design would use several smaller X2 contacts rather than one contact of the same total organic volume. In an ideal equilibrium model, repeated contacts can extract a larger overall target fraction. Whether that also improves purity depends on the relative distribution coefficients and how organic cuts are combined. This possibility was not tested and should not be represented as an observed result.

7. Measurement relationships and uncertainty

Pre-workup HPLC and final assay generally agreed on broad categorical rankings but sometimes differed appreciably in individual values. For example, batch 6 HPLC recovery was 0.3023 and final recovery 0.3284; batch 7 values were 0.3246 and 0.3271. Such differences may arise from destructive sampling, process stochasticity, measurement noise, and the fact that final and intermediate metrics can use different material contexts.

Final process-mass-balance errors were generally zero or small, including 0 for batches 9–11 and 0.00552 for batch 12. Thus there is no strong evidence that the principal trends came from catastrophic bookkeeping loss. Nevertheless, recovery denominators refer to original reactant charge, whereas purity is target divided by selected solute. A phase can therefore have high purity yet low recovery, exactly as observed after extraction and washing.

The near-unity downstream conversion and low downstream selectivity values should not be combined naively with pre-workup yield in one homogeneous kinetic model. They are conditional metrics for the selected organic phase. The most defensible separation is: pre-workup HPLC for reaction behavior; final purity and recovery for process performance.

8. Scope and unresolved alternatives

The supported conclusions apply to 0.040 mol reagent, 0.005 mol catalyst, about 0.040 L reaction solvent, 390 K, 700 rpm, and primarily 3600 s reaction time. They should not be extrapolated confidently to different concentrations, catalyst loadings, mixing regimes, pressures, or temperatures.

Important unidentifiable factors include:

• molecular identities and elementary chemical steps, because all materials are anonymous;
• activation energies and reaction orders, because charge and temperature were not systematically varied;
• catalyst–solvent interactions outside C3;
• equilibrium versus mass-transfer limitation during extraction, because only one mixing time and speed were used;
• actual full-process rankings of X0, X1, X2, and X3;
• phase-specific composition before and after each wash;
• whether late-time impurity in batch 11 arose from parallel reaction, product degradation, catalyst deactivation, or a combination;
• reproducibility, because the key workup recipes were not replicated exactly;
• whether the small apparent advantage of the 0.005 L wash is real rather than noise.

Plausible alternative models include a sequential intermediate R→P→I rather than parallel R→P and R→I; catalyst-dependent equilibrium rather than purely kinetic selectivity; incomplete extraction equilibrium; and matrix-dependent distribution coefficients that differ from the dossier anchors. The available data do not uniquely distinguish these models.

Overall, the most economical account is that C3 and S2 favor formation of the target, excessive residence time allows unwanted material to accumulate, X2 selectively partitions target into the organic phase but recovers only about half under the used phase ratio, and washing imposes a steep additional recovery penalty. This explanation accounts for the principal batch trends while acknowledging that the exact reaction network and optimum purification architecture remain unidentified.

payload.rationale: I treated reaction, partitioning, washing, and transfer as successive stages. The campaign showed that longer residence increased conversion but also accumulated byproduct, so Q02 is predicted to recover more target but have lower purity than Q01. Because these high-charge recipes use only 0.00025 mol catalyst—one twentieth of the campaign charge for 0.040 mol reagent—their recovery predictions are low and especially uncertain. For extraction, the X2 dossier coefficients and the campaign's roughly one-half target transfer into 0.030 L organic phase informed the estimates. X0 in Q03 is predicted to sacrifice recovery but give a cleaner retained fraction than X2 because its weaker partitioning, followed by washing, rejects more impurity. Smaller organic volume in Q05 similarly favors purity over recovery relative to Q06. In Q07–Q12, the reagent and catalyst are reduced together, preserving the catalyst/reagent ratio used in the campaign; recovery is therefore modeled as a fraction of the smaller original charge rather than as a small absolute amount. Washing lowers recovery and is assigned a probable, but uncertain, purity benefit. Two 0.010 L washes in Q10 are predicted to reject impurity slightly more effectively—and lose slightly more target—than one 0.020 L wash in Q09. Drying is assumed not to materially change solute ratios. The 0.97 transfer scales recovery without changing purity. Concentration in Q12 is assigned only a small purity gain and recovery loss relative to Q11 because its solute effects were not identified experimentally. Intervals are broad because C1/S2, the low catalyst charge, low-concentration reactions, X0 workup, staged washing, drying, and concentration were not directly observed in the campaign.

payload.report:
1. Supported, contradicted, and untested claims

An instance-specific prior was supplied: the material dossier gave nominal partition coefficients for X0–X3. Its claim that X2 should combine strong target transfer with favorable discrimination was directionally supported, but not fully tested. In batch 9, an X2 extraction raised purity from the pre-workup HPLC value of 0.6700 to a final 0.7670 while retaining recovery of 0.1656. However, no matched full-process experiments used X0, X1, or X3, so X2 was not experimentally established as the optimal extractant.

The self-developed claim that catalyst identity controls branching, rather than merely conversion, was supported. In the matched S0 screen, batch 3 with C2 had final conversion 0.3589 but only 0.2483 purity and 0.0972 recovery, whereas batch 4 with C3 had slightly lower conversion, 0.3299, but 0.6210 purity and 0.1883 recovery. This evidence changed the working strategy toward C3.

The claim that solvent strongly couples to reaction performance was supported. With C3 fixed, S1 and S2 in batches 6 and 7 produced recoveries of 0.3284 and 0.3271, respectively, versus 0.1883 for S0 in batch 4 and 0.1315 for S3 in batch 8. Whether C3 remains the best catalyst in S1 or S2 was untested because a catalyst-by-solvent factorial was not performed.

The initial expectation that longer heating would mainly improve useful conversion was contradicted. Batch 11 at 7200 s reached pre-workup HPLC conversion 0.7642 and yield 0.4291, but its byproduct signal rose to 0.2722 and its final purity was only 0.5882. The 3600 s C3/S2 workups had pre-workup byproduct signals around 0.15–0.17 and final purities of 0.762–0.776. That evidence shifted my explanation toward substantial late-time secondary impurity formation or product degradation.

Selective organic partitioning was supported qualitatively: batch 9 lost about half the pre-workup recovery but gained roughly 0.10 in purity after retaining the X2 organic phase. The exact equilibrium law and dossier coefficients were not validated quantitatively.

A monotonic wash-purification law was not supported. Batch 10 with a 0.005 L wash had the highest observed purity, 0.7762, but batch 12 with a 0.040 L wash had lower purity, 0.7622, and lower recovery, 0.0980. The clear result was target loss with stronger washing; a reproducible purity benefit remained unresolved. No completed batch supported the claim that the process could meet purity ≥0.80.

2. One additional discriminating experiment

I would run one C3/S2 reaction at the established charge, temperature, and mixing conditions, taking small HPLC aliquots at 1800, 3600, 5400, and 7200 s before applying the same X2 workup. This would distinguish the leading sequential explanation, P→impurity/degradation at late time, from an alternative dominated by parallel formation of target and impurity directly from reagent.

If target yield first rose and then declined while impurity increased, I would strengthen the sequential-degradation explanation and infer a finite optimum residence time. If target yield remained nondecreasing while impurity accumulated independently, I would favor parallel competing formation instead. If both target and impurity stopped changing together, catalyst deactivation or equilibrium limitation would become more plausible. If the time course were clean but final purity varied only after workup, I would shift attention from reaction chemistry to variable partitioning or washing. Replicate precision would still be needed before fitting rate constants, but a within-vessel time course would remove much of the batch-to-batch confounding present in batches 9–12.

3. Unused evidence, weak predictions, and effect of the goal

The campaign did not use the raw spectral traces or characterization artifacts; interpretation relied on processed estimates. It also left most of the supplied extractant dossier experimentally unused, because only X2 received a complete workup. Exact temperature trajectories, pressure/control options, alternative atmospheres, catalyst dose, reagent concentration, multiple contact times, staged extraction, and most drying/concentration behavior were not investigated. Batch 1 contained some evidence about a shorter, cooler reaction, but simultaneous changes in solvent volume and mishandled phase selection made it too confounded for quantitative use.

The least reliable sealed predictions are Q01–Q06 because they extrapolate to C1/S2, 400 K, and a catalyst/reagent ratio twenty times below the main campaign ratio. Q03 additionally extrapolates to an untested X0 workup, while Q05 and Q06 extrapolate phase-ratio effects from nominal coefficients rather than matched experiments. Q07–Q12 preserve the tested catalyst/reagent ratio but use much lower absolute concentrations, so concentration-dependent kinetics remain uncertain. Q10 relies on untested staged washing, and Q12 relies on an unmeasured concentration operation. Predicted purity is generally less secure than the direction of recovery changes because the campaign showed nonmonotonic wash purity.

The operating recommendation itself is also qualified: batch 10 was selected because it had the highest observed purity, not because it met the required threshold. Its 0.0092 purity advantage over unwashed batch 9 is close enough to assay and process variability that replication could reverse their ranking.

The assigned goal materially shaped evidence collection. I prioritized final purity and recovery, first screening reaction categories and then spending the remaining batches on X2 extraction and washing. That produced useful goal-directed evidence but displaced replication, catalyst-dose studies, a full catalyst–solvent interaction design, alternative extractants, and a proper kinetic time course. I do not see a direct conflict between the goal and the evidence that was collected, but the search for a purity-qualified operating recipe reduced the strength of general mechanistic identification.

recommendation.selection_rationale: Batch 10 had the highest observed final purity (0.7762) among completed batches, with recovery 0.1401 and zero reported mass-balance error. No batch reached the required 0.80 purity, so this is the closest feasible completed result; it also retains more recovery than the heavier-wash batch 12.
